text: I’ll model flow along \(z\): duct from \(z=-40\) to \(100\) mm, with the core occupying \(z=0\) to \(20\) mm. I interpret “8 mm cell width” as the **clear opening across flats**, with 1 mm shared ligaments, so adjacent cell centers are 9 mm apart. To preserve a sealed square duct wall, I’ll retain only complete hexagonal openings inside the 80 mm square; the resulting partial edge band is honeycomb solid. I’ll first create and inspect a coarse CAD representation, then mesh the same geometry with local resolution sufficient to capture the 1 mm walls.

The CAD will use exact planar hexagons; “coarse” here means only the first low-resolution visual tessellation, not a simplified cell pattern. I’ll now construct the full fluid volume and print the cell count and basic dimensions before trusting it.

The coarse CAD has 77 complete channels and one connected air volume. I’ll render the honeycomb solid inside a translucent duct envelope; this makes the channel pattern and axial placement visible more clearly than an opaque exterior view of the fluid.

The preview confirms the intended full-depth hex channels and retained edge frame. Next I’ll identify boundary faces by geometric ancestry from the original duct faces—not by bounding-box position—then verify patch areas before export. The unclaimed remainder will be the honeycomb surface.

The Boolean result contains many honeycomb side faces parallel to duct normals, so normal-only tagging would be unsafe. I’ll test overlap against the already named source duct faces and use positive coincident area as the ancestry criterion.
That API name is not present in this installed build123d version, so I’ll inspect the installed shape methods and use the supported geometric relation instead.
I’ll now measure face–source intersections. A true inherited duct face must have a finite coincident area; honeycomb faces merely touching an edge have zero area.

Coplanar face intersection returns no area in this kernel. I’ll instead require both (1) matching face normal and (2) the result-face center lying on a named source face. This still uses the source geometry directly and cannot confuse interior parallel honeycomb faces.

The explicit source-derived patches are correct, but Python wrapper identity is not a valid topological identity, so my temporary “remainder” count was invalid. I’ll use build123d’s topological equality to verify that the explicit lists do not overlap; `export_patches` will then assign the actual remainder to honeycomb walls.

Some edge cells touch the square boundary along a full hex side; those coincident surfaces correctly belong to `duct_walls`, while all internal channel and core-face surfaces remain `honeycomb_walls`. I’ll verify topological disjointness, measure the actual clear width and ligament, then export all four patches in one conformal tessellation.

I’ll now make a deliberately coarse snappyHexMesh trial: 4 mm background cells and 2 mm surface cells. The background extends 4 mm beyond the closed STL so snappy can select the interior air region cleanly; the retained point is upstream at \((0,0,-20)\) mm. This trial is for topology and patch inspection, not the final 1 mm-wall resolution.
I’ll run the coarse mesh and immediately inspect its standard mesh-quality summary and patch table.
The failure was only a missing mandatory `controlDict` write entry; no meshing computation ran. I’ll fix that now and run the existing coarse setup unchanged.
`blockMesh` now exists (17,908 coarse cells). This OpenFOAM build also requires placeholder discretization dictionaries even for snappy; I’ll add the standard minimal files and rerun only snappy.

The coarse snapped air mesh now exists with 45,880 cells and no snappy quality errors. I’ll run `checkMesh` and render a transverse slice through the core to confirm that the channel topology survived meshing.
The coarse mesh is topologically closed, but bare `checkMesh` flags 22 highly skew faces, so it is not final. Before refining/fixing it, I’ll look at the transverse core slice as requested.

The slice confirms all 77 passages and visible 1 mm ligaments, but only about four cells span each opening at this trial level. I’ll refine all surfaces to 1 mm (eight cells across each clear width), rebuild from `blockMesh`, and recheck; this should also regularize the snapped boundary faces.
The refined mesh completed with 196,736 cells and no snappy quality errors. I’ll now run the binding bare `checkMesh` and inspect the final boundary patch counts.

Bare `checkMesh` still rejects the final mesh for boundary skewness (maximum 5.67), despite all other checks passing. I’ll tighten snappy’s boundary-skewness quality limit from 20 to 4 so it backs off problematic snap displacements, then rebuild once from the coarse background.

Snappy now reports zero faces above skewness 4. I’ll rerun the binding check and, if it passes, produce one final axial cutaway image to verify the upstream duct, 20 mm core, and downstream duct connectivity.
The final bare `checkMesh` passes (`Mesh OK`), with maximum skewness 3.999 and maximum non-orthogonality 56.2°. I’ll make the final axial inspection image now.

The axial slice shows the 40 mm upstream section, 20 mm full-depth channel section, and 80 mm downstream section as one connected air mesh. No requested dimension remains unchecked; I did not run the optional stricter `checkMesh -allGeometry`, since the binding bare check passes.

The completion gate found that the exported-surface manifest omitted the same interior point used by snappy. I’ll add \((0,0,-20)\) mm to the manifest by re-exporting the unchanged patches; this does not alter the already validated mesh.

The manifest now records the validated interior meshing point. Final assumptions: “8 mm cell width” was interpreted as clear width across flats, with 9 mm center pitch; only complete hexagons were retained, leaving a solid partial edge band. All other dimensions came directly from the request.
